newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Curfew after one dead, 22 Moslems wounded in Mostar.
newsitem.headline: Curfew after one dead, 22 Moslems wounded in Mostar.

text.p: Bosnian authorities imposed a curfew in the divided city of Mostar on Monday after one person was killed and 22 were wounded in ethnic violence in which Bosnian Croats fired shots towards Moslem pilgrims trying to visit a local cemetery.

"There were 22 injured, two seriously, and one dead," NATO peace force spokesman Major Tony White said after the bloodiest ethnic violence in Mostar since NATO troops deployed in Bosnia to uphold a peace treaty ending 43 months of war.
"One of the seriously injured is being operated on now and another is in a coma."
All casualties were Moslems, he said. The dead man was a 65-year-old Moslem man, Bosnian media said.

NATO sources said shots were believed to have been fired at the Moslems during the incident and some may have been hit. But Mike Fabbro, the peace force spokesman in Mostar, told Reuters that all casualties had sustained "knife wounds".
The Croatian state news agency HINA said 18 Croat policemen were injured. There was no independent confirmation of this.
A dusk-to-dawn curfew on both sides of the divided town was ordered by Valentin Coric , a Bosnian Croat who is the Interior Minister for Hercegovina-Neretva canton, which includes Mostar.

"After a serious incident which took place in Mostar today...the security situation in the city is very complex and everything is pointing towards it becoming even more so," Radio Mostar quoted Coric as saying.
Moslem-controlled Bosnian state radio accused Croat policemen of having fired on the pilgrims while nationalist Croat media accused Moslems of provoking tensions.

The violence occurred during a confrontation between 500 Moslems heading to the Liska cemetery on the Croat side of the divided city and some 700 Croats in a Roman Catholic carnival parade who tried to block them, White said.
Sarajevo-based BH Press said several thousand Moslems took part in the procession. Monday was the second day of Bairam, an Islamic religious holiday when Moslems mourn their dead.
"The Croats started yelling and throwing stones at Moslems who tried to visit the cemetery," Fabbro said.
"The Croats had been parading (for carnival) and then the paraders went to meet the (Moslem) pilgrims. The physical movement was from the Croats towards the Moslems."
He said "one person fired three warning shots in the air" when the trouble began. "He was in civilian clothes, so we don't know if he was a policeman."
Alija Behram, a radio journalist from the Moslem-controlled eastern sector, said the mob began beating some of the Moslems and then shots rang out, spreading panic among the crowd.
"A guy close to me was shot in the forehead," Behram told Reuters by telephone. "There was panic all around us."
Carl Bildt, the international High Representative to postwar Bosnia, promptly issued a statement expressing outrage at what he called a murderous attack.

"We condemn in the strongest possible terms the indiscriminate killing of innocent civilians in Mostar today. This is murder, and must be treated as such," Bildt said in the statement from Sarajevo. "We appeal to all responsible citizens of Mostar -- Bosniaks (Moslems), Croats, Serbs or others -- for calm and dignity in a very difficult situation."
The NATO-led peace Stabilisation Force (SFOR) said it deployed some 100 Spanish troops to the town centre to defuse tensions between rival Moslem and Croat communities.

Monday's bloodshed followed weeks of escalating political battles inside the shaky Moslem-Croat federation and systematic expulsions of Moslems from western Mostar, some of them perpetrated by Croat police.
Hand grenades were heard exploding every night over the past week and in one case rifle grenades were fired at an apartment building, international police monitors reported.

Bosnian Moslems and Croats fought a war in 1993-94 until agreeing to form the federation under heavy U.S. pressure. Hardline nationalists, mainly Croats in west Mostar, have blocked efforts to reunify the town.
